---
title: "5.3 Methodology and alternatives"
order: 3
---

Adjudication is two components run in sequence. A gradient-boosted model estimates each
applicant's probability of default; a policy layer, which is not fitted to anything, turns
that PD and a handful of raw values into Approve, Refer or Decline. Both are described
here in the order the code runs them.

## The model: LightGBM

A gradient-boosted tree ensemble, fitted on the {{< var adj.n_train >}} training rows
([5.2](data.qmd#split-and-seed)) with fixed hyperparameters and the platform seed:

```python
model = LGBMClassifier(                                  # adjudication/src/train.py
    n_estimators=400, learning_rate=0.03, num_leaves=31,
    subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1, verbose=-1,
)
model.fit(X_tr, y_tr, categorical_feature=ADJ_CATEGORICAL)
```

The hyperparameters are constants, not the result of a search, and there is no early
stopping and no separate validation set: the held-out rows play no part in fitting the
trees. (They do enter the zone cutoffs, below.) The PD is `predict_proba`'s probability of the default class, uncalibrated: no
Platt or isotonic step follows the fit. How well it is calibrated is measured, zone by
zone, in [5.5](performance.qmd#adj-calibration).

## PD zones, calibrated at training {#adj-pd-zones}

After fitting, `train.py` sets the two zone cutoffs as quantiles of the model's PD — over
**all** {{< var adj.n_applicants >}} applicants, training and held-out rows together — and
writes them into `policy_config.json`:

```python
pd_full = model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]                   # adjudication/src/train.py
policy_d["t_low"] = float(round(np.quantile(pd_full, 0.55), 4))
policy_d["t_high"] = float(round(np.quantile(pd_full, 0.90), 4))
```

By construction, then, {{< var adj.zone_target.Approve >}} of all applicants' PDs fall in
the Approve zone, {{< var adj.zone_target.Refer >}} in the Refer zone and
{{< var adj.zone_target.Decline >}} in the Decline zone. The committed cutoffs are
`t_low` = {{< var adj.t_low >}} and `t_high` = {{< var adj.t_high >}}. They replace the seed
values in `shared/config.py::ADJ_POLICY`, which are only placeholders. That the cutoffs are
quantiles, and that the held-out rows are among the rows they are taken over, are
discussed in [5.4](assumptions.qmd#adj-thresholds-are-quantiles) and finding 4 of
[5.7](limitations.qmd).

## The policy layer {#adj-policy-layer}

`decide` (`adjudication/src/policy.py`) applies three steps, in this order, to every file:

1. **Hard knockouts.** Four rules on raw values. Each one that fires is recorded, and the
   file will be declined whatever its PD.
2. **PD zones.** PD at or below `t_low`: Approve. At or above `t_high`: Decline. Between:
   Refer.
3. **Refer overrides.** Three rules that apply only to a file the zones put in Approve, and
   only downgrade it to Refer. They never touch a Refer or a Decline.

Then **knockouts win**: every file with a knockout is set to Decline last, overriding steps
2 and 3. A file can therefore carry an override's reason string and still be declined: the
override fired on its Approve-zone PD, and a knockout on the same file then set the
decision. Every count of a rule in this chapter is a count of **rule hits** — files on
which the rule fired — not of decisions the rule alone determined.

```python
# --- 1. hard knockouts ---                              # adjudication/src/policy.py
m = dscr < config.dscr_floor; fire(m, f"dscr<{config.dscr_floor}"); knockout |= m
m = pubrec > config.public_records_cap; fire(m, "public_records present"); knockout |= m
m = delinq >= config.prior_delinq_cap; fire(m, f"prior_delinquencies>={config.prior_delinq_cap}"); knockout |= m
m = lev > config.leverage_cap; fire(m, f"leverage>{config.leverage_cap}"); knockout |= m

# --- 2. PD zones ---
decision = np.where(pd_model <= config.t_low, "Approve",
           np.where(pd_model >= config.t_high, "Decline", "Refer")).astype(object)

# --- 3. refer overrides (only on current Approve) ---
appr = decision == "Approve"
thin_dscr = appr & (dscr >= config.dscr_floor) & (dscr < config.dscr_refer_hi)
low_score = appr & (score < config.score_floor)
big_req = appr & (req / rev > config.req_to_rev_cap)
decision[thin_dscr | low_score | big_req] = "Refer"

# knockouts win over everything
decision[knockout] = "Decline"
```

The committed configuration, `adjudication/models/policy_config.json`:

```json
{
  "t_low": 0.0955,
  "t_high": 0.4943,
  "dscr_floor": 1.0,
  "dscr_refer_hi": 1.2,
  "public_records_cap": 0,
  "prior_delinq_cap": 3,
  "leverage_cap": 6.0,
  "req_to_rev_cap": 0.75,
  "score_floor": 600
}
```

Only `t_low` and `t_high` are set by training. The other seven are policy values copied
from `ADJ_POLICY` unchanged: limits a credit officer would set, not estimates
([5.4](assumptions.qmd#adj-knockout-limits-are-policy)).

{{< yt S3-c2 >}}

### Rule hits on the held-out applicants

{{< include ../../_generated/adj-rules.md >}}

Two rules have no hits on any of the {{< var adj.n_applicants >}} applicants: the leverage
cap and the request-to-revenue cap. Neither can fire on this data — finding 2 in
[5.7](limitations.qmd).

## Knockouts drive most Declines {#adj-knockouts-dominate}

The policy layer is not a light touch on the model. Of the {{< var adj.decline.n >}}
held-out Declines, **{{< var adj.decline.knockout_share >}} carry a hard knockout**; on the
rest, the PD alone put the file in the Decline zone. On {{< var adj.rule.knockout_overturns.n >}}
held-out files a knockout overturned the PD zone, declining a file the model had placed in
Approve or Refer. On the held-out applicants as a whole, {{< var adj.rule.any_knockout.share >}}
of files ({{< var adj.rule.any_knockout.n >}}) hit at least one knockout, while the model's
own Decline zone holds {{< var adj.zone.everyone.Decline.n >}} of them
([5.5](performance.qmd#adj-calibration)).

**Adjudication is largely a rules engine with a model attached.** The model's PD decides
the split between Approve and Refer, and a small Decline zone; the knockouts decide most of
who is declined. A validator should read the gates in [5.9](gate.qmd) with that in mind:
they measure the PD's ranking, which governs a minority of the Declines. The decisions
themselves are measured against outcomes in [5.5](performance.qmd#adj-decisions-and-outcomes).
This dominance is recorded as an observation in [5.7](limitations.qmd#adj-observations),
not a finding: the knockouts are policy, and they are doing what they say.

## Why a gradient-boosted model {#adj-why-lightgbm}

The model was built as a **challenger to the scorecard**: a flexible learner, given every
input the scorecard has plus the raw application fields and the score itself, to find
whatever signal a binned, additive model leaves behind — interactions, non-monotonic
effects, thresholds the bins smooth over. If such signal existed, the challenger would rank
the same applicants better than the scorecard.

It does not. On the same held-out applicants ([5.2](data.qmd#split-and-seed)):

| Model | Held-out AUC, same held-out applicants | Held-out AUC, same held-out booked |
|---|---|---|
| Business Credit Score (D4) | {{< var score.pop.everyone.auc >}} | {{< var score.pop.booked.auc >}} |
| Adjudication, LightGBM | {{< var adj.pop.everyone.auc >}} | {{< var adj.pop.booked.auc >}} |

The challenger is slightly below the scorecard on both populations. A paired bootstrap —
both PDs scored on the same resampled rows, {{< var score.bootstrap_n >}} times — puts the
scorecard's lead at {{< var adj.vs_score.everyone.diff >}} on all held-out applicants
(95% interval {{< var adj.vs_score.everyone.lo >}} to {{< var adj.vs_score.everyone.hi >}})
and {{< var adj.vs_score.booked.diff >}} on the booked ({{< var adj.vs_score.booked.lo >}} to
{{< var adj.vs_score.booked.hi >}}) ([5.5](performance.qmd#benchmark-the-scorecard-it-consumes)).
Both intervals contain zero: no detectable difference, and no gain. D4
records the same comparison from the scorecard's side and keeps the scorecard as the score
spine (D4.3). This chapter records the other half: the model that decides adjudication adds
no ranking power over the score it consumes, and on the booked it sits below the AUC gate
value (finding 1, [5.7](limitations.qmd)).

### Alternative considered: PD zones on the scorecard's PD

The simplest alternative is to drop the LightGBM and apply the same policy layer to the
scorecard's PD (`pd_score`) directly. With the PD-zone rule alone, the two PDs place
{{< var adj.score_zone.differ.share >}} of held-out files ({{< var adj.score_zone.differ.n >}})
in a different zone, and **{{< var adj.score_zone.opposite.n >}}** in opposite zones — no
file is Approve under one and Decline under the other. The cutoffs here are the LightGBM's;
a scorecard version would recalibrate its own at the same quantiles.

The alternative has not been adopted, and it has not been rejected on evidence either: on
this data the LightGBM buys no discrimination, and it costs the exact reason codes (below).
What it does give is a model that can use inputs the scorecard does not have —
`requested_amount`, `term_months`, `loan_purpose`, `collateral_flag` — should a real book
show them to carry signal. On the generated data none of them has a causal role in default;
`requested_amount` only borrows revenue's signal ([D2](../d2-data.qmd)). The choice is recorded as an open question for the next
redevelopment ([5.8](monitoring.qmd#adj-redevelopment-triggers)), not as a finding.

## Reason codes: SHAP, not weights of evidence {#adj-reason-codes}

The scorecard's reason codes are exact by construction: its log-odds are an intercept plus
one WoE × coefficient term per feature, and the adverse reasons are the largest terms
(D4.3). A tree ensemble has no such decomposition. Its reasons come from SHAP values:

```python
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(model)                    # adjudication/src/train.py
sv = explainer.shap_values(X_te.iloc[:50])
sv = sv[1] if isinstance(sv, list) else sv
_ = top_adverse_shap(sv, ADJ_FEATURE_COLUMNS, k=3)
```

`top_adverse_shap` keeps, for each file, the three features with the largest positive SHAP
value — the largest pushes towards default — and drops any non-positive one. `TreeExplainer`
is exact for a tree ensemble in one sense: the base value plus the SHAP values reproduces the
model's log-odds. The v2 workbench serves that decomposition as a ledger (`app/v2/ledgers.py`),
and the test suite checks the identity on a sample of applicants
(`tests/test_app_v2.py::test_shap_is_exactly_additive`); the ledger itself asserts nothing.
It is still an *attribution method*, with choices of its own: how credit is shared between
correlated features is one of them, and a validator has to validate the method as well as the
model. `train.py` runs it on the first {{< var adj.train_shap_rows >}} held-out rows as a sanity check only; nothing is gated on it.

The sharpest case is the model's two strongest inputs. `business_score` and `pd_score` are
two transforms of the scorecard's single log-odds: over all {{< var adj.n_applicants >}}
applicants, sorted by `pd_score`, `business_score` rises {{< var adj.score_pd.order_breaks >}}
times. They are one signal in two columns, and SHAP splits its credit between them. A file
whose top-three reasons include both `pd_score` and `business_score` has been given one reason twice
— and a reason that is itself a model output, not a fact about the business. What that means
for adverse-action notices and for the dependency on D4 is in
[5.5](performance.qmd#adj-reasons-among-declines).

## Feature selection

None, in the sense of a search: `ADJ_FEATURE_COLUMNS` is a fixed list
([5.2](data.qmd#adj-features)). LightGBM's column subsampling (`colsample_bytree=0.8`)
draws a random subset of the columns for each tree, which is regularisation, not selection.
